body.text: When Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) president Sukhbir Singh Badal returned to political stage in Sri Muktsar Sahib district on August 26 (after surviving an attack at Hazur Sahib in Maharashtra’s Nanded on August 13), he did not target the ruling AAP or the Congress. Instead, he targeted Amritpal Singh, the jailed Lok Sabha MP from Khadoor Sahib, and his party, the Akali Dal Waris Punjab De (Successor of Punjab). The latter is seeking to enter the same “Panthic” space in Punjab’s politics that has for long been dominated by the SAD.

Addressing the “Save Punjab” rally, Badal alleged that the Waris Punjab De represented the same forces that destroyed the peace of Punjab in the 1980s, killed former SAD president Sant Harchand Singh Longowal and party leader Bhai Shaminder Singh, and attacked Gurcharan Singh Tohra during insurgency.

Waris Punjab De was formally launched by supporters of Amritpal Singh, with him as party president, in January 2025 during the Mela Maghi festival in Sri Muktsar Sahib. He is a radical preacher and pro-Khalistan separatist who has been incarcerated under the National Security Act (NSA) in Dibrugarh Jail, Assam. The party was announced by his father, Tarsem Singh, alongside Faridkot MP Sarabjeet Singh Khalsa and a group of radical Sikh activists.

At least four Akali factions are now battling for Panthic votes ahead of State Assembly elections: the SAD; the Waris Punjab De; the SAD (Simranjit Singh Mann) or the SAD (Amritsar); and the SAD (Resurgent) or the SAD (Punar Surjit), a breakaway faction of dissident leaders from the SAD. (The latter was formed in August 2025 after a severe internal crisis in the party in the wake of directives and edicts from Akal Takht, the highest Sikh religious authority based in the Golden Temple in Amritsar.)

For decades, the SAD enjoyed complete monopoly over the mainstream Panthic space. However, it lost its exclusive claim because of the repeated sacrilege controversies during the party’s rule, especially from 2012 to 2017. These years also saw a growth in crimes and drug menace. Further, Badal’s political standing suffered amid allegations that his private business interests intertwined with his party’s governance in the State. In December 2024, the Akal Takht declared Badal a “tankhaiya” (guilty of religious misconduct). Badal pleaded guilty. The Akal Takht also revoked the “Fakhr-e-Quam” (pride of the community) title that was previously awarded to his father, Parkash Singh Badal, a five-time Chief Minister of Punjab.

While performing penance at the Golden Temple in December 2024, Badal escaped a bid on his life. Mainstream Sikh institutions and leadership unequivocally condemned the act, and hard line elements and observers noted it as a dangerous manifestation of Panthic anger against the Badals.

Jagtar Singh, a political commentator and author, traced the beginning of this shift to much earlier. He argued that the SAD began moving away from Panthic politics during its Moga conference in 1996, and an eventual disconnect contributed to the party’s marginalisation. This culminated in its historic low of just three seats in the 2022 Assembly election. Jagtar Singh, however, cautioned against treating Panthic politics and electoral politics as synonymous. The two, he said, generally “co-exist and complement each other” but can also operate independently. After the SAD’s decline, he argued, the Panthic constituency was taken up by several groups that did not themselves contest elections.

The proliferation of Panthic formations may not necessarily result in a fragmented Panthic vote. Jagtar Singh asserted that Panthic voters have historically demonstrated the ability to consolidate electorally even when several groups compete for their support. He said that after backing the AAP in 2022, sections of this constituency are now moving towards Waris Punjab De. “The Panthic voters rarely miscalculate or fragment their strength. When the ballots are cast, the Panthic vote traditionally moves as one,” he said.

There are signs that the process Jagtar Singh described as Panthic consolidation may already be underway. While Waris Punjab De is represented by a younger leadership, it rose to prominence through confrontational politics. Besides Amritpal Singh, the party has another Lok Sabha MP, Sarabjeet Singh Khalsa. Son of Beant Singh, one of the bodyguards who assassinated former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. Khalsa won the Faridkot constituency in the 2024 general election as an independent candidate, defeating an AAP candidate.
A new political constituency

The insurgency-era legacy is returning to Punjab’s political discourse. Waris Punjab De appears to be trying to create a new political constituency rather than just reclaiming the old space occupied by the SAD. On August 10, the party announced Satwant Singh as its first candidate for the election due early next year. He is the son of Kehar Singh, who was executed in 1989 for his role in assassinating Indira Gandhi.

On August 21, Punjab witnessed a Statewide shutdown (Punjab bandh) triggered by Panthic bodies and supported by organisations like Waris Punjab De demanding the immediate release or parole of long-term Sikh prisoners (Bandi Singhs).

Meanwhile, Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann met Governor Gulab Chand Kataria and sought a 10-day parole for Jagtar Singh Hawara, convicted in the 1995 assassination of former Punjab Chief Minister Beant Singh, on humanitarian grounds to meet his ailing mother. Former Union Minister and BJP leader Ravneet Singh Bittu, grandson of Beant Singh, who is otherwise a vocal opponent of leniency towards such convicts, also backed Bhagwant Mann’s request on humanitarian grounds.

Ahead of the Assembly election, the SAD (Simranjit Singh Mann), is positioning itself as a hard-line Panthic alternative. It has started announcing candidates to contest the 117 Vidhan Sabha seats. The party was at its high when Simranjit Singh Mann won the Sangrur Lok Sabha byelection in 2022, but it lost the seat in the 2024 Lok Sabha election. It has always maintained an anti-centre and anti-establishment stand and has advocated for greater State autonomy. On several occasions, it has openly supported Khalistan, a sovereign Sikh state. It has, time and again, called for the immediate release and parole of Bandi Singhs.

The SAD-BJP alliance lasted from 1996 until the farmers’ agitation against three controversial farm Bills in 2020. The coalition formed government in Punjab in 1997, 2007, and 2012. The meeting between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and SAD president Badal in Delhi on August 7 has now fueled speculations that the two parties may ally again.

Although the BJP’s State leadership says it will contest all 117 seats alone, statements by SAD leaders and media reports point to back-channel discussions. In fact, political networks of the two parties have already started supporting each other. During the student council elections held at Panjab University, Chandigarh, on August 31, the student wing of the SAD, the Student Organisation of India, openly supported the Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad candidate Ankit Bidhan, who was subsequently elected as the president of the Panjab University Campus Students Council.

The SAD (Punar Surjit), meanwhile, could also provide a potential bridge between the BJP and sections of the Panthic space. It has indicated openness to talks with the BJP while insisting on “non-negotiable”, “clearly defined” Panth and Punjab-centric conditions. Although the party’s president Giani Harpreet Singh, a former Akal Takht Jathedar, gives the faction a religious legitimacy and senior Akali pedigree, the party lacks an organisational footprint despite its symbolic claims over Panthic politics. The outfit’s agenda is to restore traditional Panthic values alongside inclusive governance and socio-economic reforms. Addressing a press conference on August 30, Harpreet Singh said, “We are open to an alliance with the BJP, but it will be agenda-based… we will not be part of any alliance with the party led by the Badal family.”

Given Punjab’s diverse demographic profile, Panthic votes do not automatically translate into a Panthic government, as per observers. Sikhs form a majority, but Punjab also has a large Hindu and Scheduled Caste population. Moreover, religious identity does not always determine electoral choice as it became clear in the previous State Assembly election in which the AAP saw a landslide victory.

Nevertheless, given the possible Panthic vote consolidation, Ashutosh Kumar, head of the Department of Political Science at Panjab University, said that the Congress could emerge as the biggest loser because the Panthic vote has traditionally been hostile to the party. Kumar points to the enduring political legacy of Operation Blue Star, the 1984 Delhi massacre, and the Congress’s failure to deliver on the Chandigarh commitment under the 1985 Rajiv-Longowal Accord. In his assessment, the SAD would logically be the biggest casualty of such consolidation, but the party is currently “nowhere in the contention”.

Meanwhile, if the traditional SAD-BJP coalition remains broken, the BJP has an incentive to build its own direct support base among sections of Punjab’s Sikh and rural electorate. Kumar believes, for instance, that there is scope for the BJP to consolidate support among sections of Khatri and Arora communities associated with trade, industry, and business, particularly if it is perceived that the party will offer a more investment and business-friendly environment. According to him, the balance of electoral advantage has shifted significantly since the earlier SAD-BJP alliance. “The BJP has everything to gain from the alliance,” he said, adding that while an alliance could help the SAD, it may not substantially alter its electoral outcome. Kumar also corroborated observers like Jagtar Singh and stated that Waris Punjab De could hurt the AAP the most, particularly in constituencies where the AAP absorbed sections of the traditional Panthic vote in 2022.

The big question, therefore, is not the number of Panthic groups in the fray, but the direction in which Panthic voters will eventually turn en masse. And yet, Panthic votes alone cannot win Punjab. The State’s social diversity, its rural-urban divide, and voters’ concerns over jobs, drugs, governance, and economic development will surely matter just as much. The 2027 election will be a test not merely of who captures the Panthic space, but also of whether they can turn it into a broader political coalition and emerge as a credible Statewide political force.
